messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Yusef, a 78-year-old Middle Eastern environmental scientist, came to treatment after months of carrying a memory that would not settle into the past. Years earlier, while working in the field on a remote riverbank, he had made a misjudgment with equipment and accidentally caused a serious injury to another man, a colleague who had been standing too close when a load shifted. The scene had unfolded fast and helplessly: shouting, blood, the shock of seeing someone he respected collapse because of his error. In the days afterward, what stayed with Yusef was not just what he had done but the impossibility of fully putting it into words. He could tell people, in outline, that an accident had happened, but when he tried to explain it in detail he felt stuck, as if the facts were there but the language would not come. He described the memory as so extreme that it seemed hard to believe it had really happened to him, as though it belonged to someone else’s life. Yet at other moments it came back with a crushing immediacy, and he would feel as if he were right back at the riverbank, watching the injury unfold in the present tense rather than remembering it from a distance.

Over time he learned that certain ordinary moments could pull him straight into that state. Heavy breathing was the most unsettling; if his wife was short of breath after climbing stairs, or if he heard his own breath catch while gardening, his attention snapped to the sound and the scene at the riverbank flooded back with full force. He also found that feeling happy or relaxed could suddenly turn unstable. A calm afternoon with his wife, or a brief sense of ease while sitting on the porch, could be enough to make the memory intrude, as if his mind did not permit him to rest without reopening what had happened. Physical affection was similarly fraught. When his wife reached for him in a hug, he often stiffened, not because he did not want closeness but because the sensation and nearness seemed to activate the same wordless, almost unbelievable recollection of the injury. In those moments the memory did not arrive as a story he could tell; it arrived as a vivid, present-tense experience that overwhelmed his ability to organize it into language.

Because those experiences were so jarring, Yusef gradually shaped his days around them. He became wary of situations in which someone might breathe heavily nearby, and he would subtly step back in conversations, at home as well as in the community center where he occasionally volunteered on environmental projects, if he noticed a person sounding winded. He also began to distrust ease itself. When he caught himself feeling content, he sometimes became tense almost immediately, waiting for the old scene to break in. That made relaxation hard to trust, and his wife noticed that even gentle affection could leave him distant for a while afterward. What had once been comforting now felt risky, because the slightest warmth, softness, or physical closeness could reopen the same memory he could not adequately describe. The result was a narrowing of his world: fewer spontaneous embraces, less sitting quietly with his wife, and a growing sense that the accident still had authority over the present.

By the time he sought help, Yusef was exhausted by how often the memory would seize him and how unreal it continued to feel, despite its force. He was frightened by the way heavy breathing, happiness, and a loving hug could all become doorways back into that moment at the riverbank. What brought him to treatment was a recent evening when his wife embraced him after good news about a family gathering, and he suddenly felt himself pulled back into the accident with such intensity that he had to leave the room. He said he was no longer sure how to live with a mind that could not keep the event in the past, and he hoped for help in finding words for what happened and some way to feel, at last, that it belonged to memory rather than to the room he was standing in.
